items.title: [Real Estate 101 #11] Almost Nobody Pays Cash: The Three Ways Real Estate Gets Financed
items.body:
> Real estate runs on borrowed money — a mortgage buys the house you live in, project finance builds the tower downtown, and a REIT lets you own a slice of both for the price of one share.

## Today's Concept

Real estate is expensive and mostly illiquid, so almost every deal — from a starter home to a $400 million office tower — is a financing deal wearing a building costume. There are three main channels, and they differ mainly in **what the lender is actually betting on**.

**1. The mortgage (household level).** You borrow against a property that already exists. The lender looks at two things: the collateral and you.

```
LTV = loan amount / property value
DTI = monthly debt payments / gross monthly income
```

A conventional loan typically wants LTV at or below 80% (that's a 20% down payment) and DTI in the low-to-mid 40s, sometimes up to 50% with strong credit and reserves. Go above 80% LTV and you'll usually pay private mortgage insurance (PMI) until you get back down to 80%. The key structural fact: it's **recourse to you**. Miss payments and the lender can foreclose on the house *and*, in many states, come after you for the shortfall.

**2. Project finance / construction lending (development level).** A developer building something that doesn't exist yet can't pledge a finished building. So the loan is underwritten against the **project's own projected cash flow**, and it's typically held in a single-purpose entity that owns nothing else. Money is released in draws as construction hits milestones, not in one lump sum. It's often non-recourse or limited-recourse — if the project fails, the lender takes the project, not the developer's other assets. That's why lenders demand real equity underneath (commonly 30–40% of total cost) and a coverage cushion:

```
DSCR = net operating income / annual debt service
```

Most lenders want DSCR of at least 1.20–1.25 once the building is leased up. Below 1.0 the building doesn't cover its own loan.

**3. REITs (public market level).** A real estate investment trust owns income-producing property (an *equity REIT*) or property loans (a *mortgage REIT*), and sells shares of itself. To keep REIT tax status it must distribute at least **90% of taxable income** to shareholders, hold at least 75% of assets in real estate-type assets, and draw at least 75% of gross income from rents, mortgage interest, and property sales. In exchange, it avoids corporate-level tax on distributed income. Practical translation: high dividend payout, low retained earnings, and dividends that are generally taxed as **ordinary income** rather than at qualified-dividend rates.

The thread running through all three is **leverage** — and leverage cuts both directions, which most people only half-remember.

## In Everyday Life

Say you're buying a $350,000 house in Columbus, Ohio. You put 20% down ($70,000) and borrow $280,000 on a 30-year fixed. At 6.5%, principal and interest run about **$1,770 a month** — before taxes, insurance, and any HOA. Over the full 30 years you'd pay roughly **$357,000 in interest**, more than the amount you borrowed. That's the price of not waiting 15 years to save cash.

Now the leverage math. Your $70,000 controls a $350,000 asset — 5x. If the house appreciates 10% to $385,000, your equity goes from $70,000 to $105,000: a **50% gain**. If it drops 10% to $315,000, your equity falls to $35,000: a **50% loss**. Same 10% move, five times the impact on your money. Nothing about the house changed; the loan did that.

Two blocks away, a developer is putting up a 200-unit apartment building. Total cost: $60 million. A bank lends $40 million (about 65% loan-to-cost), released in draws as the foundation, frame, and finishes get completed; the developer brings $20 million of equity and preferred capital. Nobody's personal house backs this. When the building stabilizes and throws off, say, $3.9 million of net operating income against roughly $2.9 million of annual debt service, DSCR lands near 1.35 — comfortable. At a 6% cap rate that NOI values the building around $65 million, so a $60 million cost turns into roughly $5 million of gain on $20 million of equity. Illustrative, not typical: a nine-month construction delay, a rate move, or lease-up at 88% instead of 95% can erase that spread entirely.

And who buys that stabilized building? Often a REIT — one of the roughly 200 publicly traded U.S. REITs listed on the NYSE and Nasdaq. Which means the same apartment complex you drive past is something you can own a sliver of from a brokerage account for the price of one share, collecting your cut of the rent as a quarterly dividend, without ever fixing a water heater.

## 3-Line Summary

1. A mortgage lends against an existing property and against **you** (LTV + DTI, usually with recourse); project finance lends against a **future building's cash flow**, held in its own entity, usually with limited recourse and a DSCR test.
2. Leverage multiplies percentage returns in both directions — 20% down means a 10% price move becomes a 50% move in your equity.
3. A REIT converts illiquid buildings into tradable shares; the 90% distribution requirement is why REITs pay big dividends and why those dividends are generally taxed as ordinary income.

## ✅ Self Quiz

**1.** You buy a $400,000 property with a $320,000 loan. What is the LTV, and would you typically owe PMI on a conventional loan?
  (a) 80%, no PMI   (b) 80%, PMI required   (c) 125%, no PMI   (d) 20%, PMI required

**2. True or False:** A REIT must distribute at least 90% of its taxable income to shareholders to maintain REIT tax status.

**3.** A project has $2.4 million in net operating income and $2.0 million in annual debt service. Which statement is correct?
  (a) DSCR is 0.83 — the project cannot cover its debt
  (b) DSCR is 1.20 — the project covers its debt with a 20% cushion
  (c) DSCR is 4.4 — this is the cap rate
  (d) DSCR cannot be calculated without the purchase price

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **LTV (Loan-to-Value)** — Loan amount divided by property value; the lender's primary measure of collateral cushion.
- **DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio)** — Net operating income divided by annual debt service; below 1.0 the property can't pay its own loan.
- **Non-recourse loan** — A loan where the lender's remedy on default is limited to the pledged property, not the borrower's other assets.
- **Takeout (permanent) loan** — Long-term financing that replaces a short-term construction loan once the building is completed and leased.
- **Cap rate** — Net operating income divided by property price; a rough yield measure used to value income property (`Cap rate = NOI / price`).
- **REIT** — A company owning income-producing real estate or real estate debt that avoids corporate-level tax by distributing at least 90% of taxable income.

---

*Answers: **1. (a)** — $320,000 / $400,000 = 80% LTV, which is exactly the conventional threshold, so PMI is generally not required; PMI kicks in above 80% LTV (less than 20% down). **2. True** — the 90% distribution requirement is a core REIT qualification test, alongside the 75% asset and 75% income tests. **3. (b)** — $2.4M / $2.0M = 1.20 DSCR, meaning income exceeds debt payments by 20%; most lenders set a floor around 1.20–1.25. Cap rate is a separate calculation and needs the price.*

items.title: One Shot, Six Months, Ten Countries: Why the World's Best HIV Prevention Drug Isn't Reaching Everyone Who Needs It
items.body:
## A Breakthrough Drug Meets a Familiar Bottleneck

For decades, HIV prevention has meant daily pills, regular clinic visits, and the kind of routine that's easy to fall off of. Lenacapavir, the twice-yearly injectable developed by Gilead Sciences, was supposed to change that math entirely. Two shots a year, near-complete protection in clinical trials, and a level of convenience that public health researchers have called one of the most significant advances in HIV prevention in a generation.

The catch isn't the science. It's getting the drug into arms.

## What Gilead Promised

Under pressure from global health advocates and in partnership with international health organizations, Gilead agreed to supply lenacapavir at no profit to a group of low- and middle-income countries where HIV rates remain highest, particularly across parts of sub-Saharan Africa. The company also licensed generic manufacturers to produce lower-cost versions for broader distribution once regulatory approvals and production capacity catch up.

On paper, it was a rare example of a pharmaceutical company moving quickly to align pricing with public health need rather than waiting years for generic competition to force the issue.

## Where the Rollout Is Stalling

In practice, according to clinicians and health officials involved in early distribution, the picture has been uneven. Some clinics in participating countries report shelves stocked with the injectable and ready to enroll patients. Others say they've been told to expect shipments only as late as November, leaving providers unable to give patients a firm timeline and, in some cases, unable to start new patients on the drug at all.

Health workers describe a mix of causes: limited global manufacturing capacity for a genuinely new type of injectable, regulatory approval processes that move at different speeds from country to country, and the logistical complexity of distributing a temperature-sensitive product across health systems with very different levels of infrastructure. None of these are unusual problems in global drug rollouts — but they are colliding with unusually high expectations for a drug that trial data suggested could meaningfully bend the trajectory of new HIV infections.

## Why the Timing Matters

Public health advocates note that delays are not neutral. Every month a clinic goes without supply is a month where people who might have started prevention instead go without it, relying on daily pills that are effective but harder to sustain for many people over long periods. International health organizations have been vocal about wanting the initial rollout to reach the countries and populations most affected by HIV as quickly as possible, arguing that early, well-targeted access can have outsized effects on transmission over time.

Gilead and its distribution partners have generally acknowledged that scaling manufacturing and logistics for a first-of-its-kind product takes time, and have pointed to expansion plans intended to close gaps between countries in the coming months.

## The Bigger Picture

Lenacapavir's rollout is being closely watched not just as a public health story but as a test case for how quickly the industry can move when a company commits to no-profit pricing in lower-income markets. If the supply chain smooths out in the coming months, advocates say it could become a model for future drug launches. If the gaps persist into next year, it risks becoming another example of a promising medical breakthrough arriving unevenly — available in theory long before it's available in practice.

For now, the answer likely varies clinic by clinic. Some patients in eligible countries can get an appointment for lenacapavir this month. Others are being asked to check back after the new year begins its final stretch, hoping the supply catches up with the science.

*This article is for general informational purposes and does not constitute medical advice. Readers with questions about HIV prevention options should consult a qualified healthcare provider.*

items.title: Five Days to 50%: Inside the New Tariff Deadline Squeezing Canada, Brazil and 60 Other Trading Partners
items.body:
Two trade actions that have been building quietly for weeks are now converging on a single, consequential date. Starting August 19, a 50% tariff on a wide swath of Canadian goods takes effect, layering on top of tariffs already imposed on Brazil and dozens of other countries over forced-labor concerns in global supply chains. Together, the two measures touch products from dairy and wine to furniture, motor vehicles and clothing — and they rely on legal authority the United States has almost never used in this way before.

## The Canada Deadline: August 19

In late July, the White House signed proclamations invoking Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a Depression-era provision that lets the president impose additional duties of up to 50% on goods from a country found to discriminate against U.S. commerce. It is a tool with almost no modern precedent — and it is now set to apply a 50% surcharge to a specific list of Canadian imports beginning August 19.

The headline categories are dairy, alcoholic beverages and motor vehicles, but trade advisories describe a longer list that also includes wine, furniture, plywood, cement, hockey sticks, fishing rods, seeds and clothing. Notably, goods that normally qualify for duty-free treatment under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) are not exempt from this new tariff — origin under the trade pact does not shield covered products from the Section 338 duty.

Trade groups estimate the exposure at roughly $20 billion, a slice of the more than $380 billion in goods the U.S. imported from Canada last year. For companies that source dairy ingredients, packaged alcohol or finished furniture from Canadian suppliers, the deadline leaves only days to adjust purchasing plans, renegotiate contracts, or absorb the added cost.

## The Forced-Labor Tariffs: 60 Countries, Two Rates

Running alongside the Canada action is a separate and broader measure. Earlier this summer, the U.S. Trade Representative's office released findings from Section 301 investigations into 60 trading economies, examining whether each country bans — and effectively enforces bans on — imports made with forced labor. The conclusion: most fell short, and USTR proposed new tariffs as a result.

Under the rollout, roughly a dozen economies that maintain at least a partial prohibition or have committed to reciprocal-trade enforcement steps face a 10% tariff, while the majority of the 60 countries face a steeper 12.5% rate. Brazil is among the economies assigned the higher tier; its government has publicly pushed back, calling the action unjustified. Unlike the Canada tariffs, which take effect August 19, the forced-labor duties began landing on shipments in late July, meaning many importers are already absorbing the cost.

## Why Now, and Why These Tools

Both actions share a common thread: each relies on a legal mechanism that has sat largely dormant for decades. Section 338 has essentially never been used to impose duties at this scale, while Section 301's forced-labor framing marks a shift from its more familiar role in disputes over intellectual property or subsidies. Trade attorneys tracking the rollout note that the unusual legal basis for both measures could make them targets for legal challenges or future negotiation, even as they take effect on schedule for now.

## What It Means Going Forward

For everyday consumers, the near-term effect is likely to show up gradually — in the price of Canadian cheese, whisky and furniture, and in goods imported from the 60 affected economies, from apparel to electronics components. For businesses, the bigger challenge is the compressed timeline: importers have had only weeks, not months, to map which SKUs are covered, recalculate landed costs and decide whether to pass increases on to customers.

Because tariff schedules, product exclusion lists and country-specific rates can change on short notice — through litigation, bilateral talks or further executive action — businesses and consumers with a direct stake in these categories should verify current requirements through official U.S. Trade Representative and Customs and Border Protection guidance, or with qualified trade counsel, rather than relying on any single news summary. The situation remains fluid, and the coming days are likely to bring further clarification from both Washington and the affected trading partners.

items.title: The Plea That Could End One Trial and Start Another: Inside Luigi Mangione's Friday Federal Court Reckoning
items.body:
A federal courtroom in Manhattan is set to become the center of one of the most closely watched criminal cases in recent memory this Friday, as Luigi Mangione is expected to enter a guilty plea to federal stalking charges connected to the killing of UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson. According to court filings and people familiar with the proceedings, the expected plea would resolve one track of a sprawling, two-front prosecution — while potentially reshaping the far more consequential murder case still pending in New York state court.

## A Case Split Across Two Systems

Since his arrest in December 2024, Mangione has faced parallel prosecutions that rarely move in lockstep. New York state prosecutors charged him with murder and related offenses in state court, while federal prosecutors separately pursued charges that include stalking and firearms offenses tied to the same underlying events. Legal analysts have long noted that running two prosecutions simultaneously creates procedural complexity, from evidentiary overlap to scheduling conflicts, and can also create leverage — and risk — for both sides at the negotiating table.

Reports describing the anticipated Friday proceeding indicate the plea would be limited to the federal stalking counts, not the more serious federal charges that have drawn national attention, including those that prosecutors have previously signaled could carry the most severe penalties available under federal law. Defense attorneys have not confirmed the full scope of any agreement, and terms described in advance of a formal hearing can change until they are entered on the record before a judge.

## Why a Partial Plea Matters

Legal observers say a guilty plea to a narrower set of federal charges would not, by itself, resolve Mangione's overall legal exposure. The New York state murder case is expected to proceed independently, governed by its own timeline, evidentiary rules, and jury pool. A federal plea could, however, influence that case in subtle ways: it may affect what statements or admissions become part of the public record, shape pretrial motions from either side, and factor into how state prosecutors calibrate their own strategy in the months ahead.

Defense attorneys in high-profile dual-jurisdiction cases sometimes use a plea on lesser federal counts as a way to narrow the scope of a client's total exposure, while prosecutors may accept such an arrangement if it secures a documented admission without the cost, delay, and uncertainty of a full trial. Neither outcome is guaranteed here, and any characterization of motive on either side remains speculative until attorneys and the court confirm the terms publicly.

## A Story That Has Drawn National Attention

Thompson's killing in December 2024 drew intense public and media scrutiny, in part because of its connection to broader public debate over the U.S. health insurance industry. That debate has continued alongside the legal proceedings, and commentary about the case — including online reaction — has at times overshadowed the facts of the prosecution itself. Legal experts caution that public sentiment, whatever form it takes, has no bearing on the presumption of innocence for charges that remain contested, or on the procedural fairness owed to any defendant in the American justice system.

Court officials have not released a detailed public schedule beyond confirming that proceedings are expected Friday, and both prosecution and defense teams have generally declined to comment ahead of the hearing, consistent with standard practice in active federal cases.

## What Comes Next

If the plea proceeds as anticipated, attention will shift almost immediately to the New York murder case, where no trial date has been widely confirmed as of this writing. Sentencing on any federal counts would typically follow at a later hearing, separate from Friday's proceeding, giving both sides time to file additional briefs.

For now, the central question facing legal observers is not whether Friday's hearing resolves Mangione's legal jeopardy — by most accounts, it will not — but how it recalibrates the far larger and more consequential case still to come. Court watchers, family members of those affected, and the public are likely to keep close watch on developments as they unfold in the weeks ahead.

*This report reflects publicly available information as of publication and may be updated as court proceedings continue. Details of any plea agreement remain subject to confirmation by the court.*
